case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a federal court sitting in diversity must enforce Delaware’s medical-negligence “affidavit of merit” (AOM) pre-suit/early-suit filing requirement, or whether the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure displace it such that a plaintiff may proceed without complying.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Delaware’s healthcare-negligence Affidavit of Merit requirement (the Delaware AOM statute governing medical-negligence actions, requiring an expert affidavit/certificate as a condition to proceed) and its interaction with the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure (principally Rules 8, 9, 11, 12, 15, and 56) under the Erie/Hanna framework (Rules Enabling Act analysis).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Berk argues that Delaware’s AOM requirement is a state procedural screening device that conflicts with, and therefore is displaced by, the Federal Rules governing pleading, filing, and sanctions in federal court. In his view, applying the AOM statute in federal diversity actions improperly adds a heightened, state-created filing prerequisite beyond what Rules 8/11/12 require, effectively functioning as a merits/evidence gate at the outset. He contends Erie/Hanna requires uniform federal procedure and that enforcing the AOM statute in federal court undermines the Federal Rules’ calibrated system for testing plausibility, managing discovery, and sanctioning baseless claims, while risking dismissal of otherwise valid claims on a technicality.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Choy and Beebe Medical Center argue that Delaware’s AOM requirement is substantive (or at least outcome-determinative in the Erie sense) because it is tightly bound to the state’s definition and enforcement of medical-negligence liability and serves core state policy goals (screening non-meritorious malpractice claims, reducing defensive medicine, stabilizing insurance/healthcare costs). They contend there is no direct collision with any Federal Rule because the AOM requirement operates as a state-law condition on maintaining a malpractice action (or a precondition to proceeding), not as an alternative federal pleading standard. Under Erie and Hanna, they argue, failing to apply the Delaware AOM rule would invite forum shopping (federal court as an AOM-free bypass) and produce inequitable administration of the laws, so federal courts must enforce it in diversity cases.
key_precedents: Shady Grove Orthopedic Associates, P.A. v. Allstate Insurance Co.
Burlington Northern Railroad Co. v. Woods
Gasperini v. Center for Humanities, Inc.

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point remains that Delaware’s AOM functions as an early merits screen that resembles—and could be said to disrupt—the Federal Rules’ integrated pleading and dismissal framework (Rules 8, 12, 15, 56). But under Hanna and Burlington Northern, the antecedent question is whether any Federal Rule is sufficiently broad to answer the precise question in dispute and leave no room for Delaware’s requirement; Justice Barrett’s textual point about Rule 11 expressly contemplating affidavits required by “a rule or statute” strongly supports construing the Rules to coexist with state-law merit-certification conditions rather than to preempt them. Justice Kagan’s and Justice Gorsuch’s Walker analogy reinforces that, absent a direct collision, Erie’s twin aims carry real weight here because ignoring the AOM predictably invites forum shopping and inequitable administration by creating an AOM-free federal bypass. A narrow holding limited to Delaware’s specific AOM mechanism and diversity jurisdiction best avoids unnecessary REA/Shady Grove pronouncements while preserving institutional legitimacy.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right that Delaware’s affidavit-of-merit functions as an early merits screen and can feel like a heightened pleading regime, but under Hanna and Burlington Northern the dispositive question is textual: whether any Federal Rule is sufficiently broad to answer the same question and leave no room for the state condition. As Justice Barrett emphasizes, Rule 11 expressly contemplates affidavits when a “rule or statute” requires them, which undermines the claim that the Federal Rules categorically occupy this field or forbid Delaware’s mechanism. Walker’s logic, as Justice Gorsuch notes, fits: the Rules govern federal pleading and motion practice, while Delaware may define the preconditions for maintaining its state-created medical-negligence claim absent a direct collision. With no collision, Erie’s twin aims favor applying Delaware’s requirement to prevent an AOM-free federal bypass, and Sotomayor’s access concerns cannot justify expanding the Rules beyond their text and original public meaning.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s best point is that Delaware’s AOM functions as a front-loaded merits screen that seems to intrude on the Federal Rules’ pleading and dismissal scheme (Rules 8, 12, 15), potentially creating a practical “heightened filing” requirement. But as Justice Barrett explains, Rule 11’s text expressly contemplates affidavit/verification demands imposed by a “rule or statute,” which makes it hard to say the Federal Rules occupy this field so completely that any state certification prerequisite necessarily collides. Walker and Burlington Northern, as invoked by the Chief Justice and Justice Gorsuch, reinforce that we should read the Rules at the right level of generality: they regulate federal pleading and motion practice, not whether a State may condition continuation of a state-created malpractice claim on early expert support. With no direct collision, Erie’s twin aims strongly favor applying Delaware’s AOM to avoid an AOM-free federal bypass, and Sotomayor’s access-to-justice concerns—while real—do not justify stretching the Rules’ text to preempt the State’s gatekeeping policy.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: I take Chief Justice Roberts’s “no direct collision” framing seriously, but I don’t think we can define the “question in dispute” so narrowly that Delaware’s AOM is treated as merely a freestanding ‘condition’ on a claim rather than what it functionally is: a mandatory, front-loaded expert screen enforced through dismissal at the pleading stage, occupying the same field Rules 8, 12, and 15 structure for initiating suit, testing sufficiency, and curing defects. Justice Barrett’s reliance on Rule 11’s ‘unless a rule or statute specifically states otherwise’ clause does not, to my mind, dissolve the collision; it prevents an across-the-board federal verification requirement, but it does not mean state law may superadd a dismissal-triggering affidavit regime that recalibrates when a federal action may proceed and be amended under the Rules. Walker, as Justice Kagan and Justice Gorsuch invoke it, is distinguishable because it concerned Rule 3’s limited ‘commencement’ function for federal timing, not a state device designed to terminate claims before discovery in a way that mirrors and displaces federal plausibility and amendment practice. On my pragmatic view, allowing AOM dismissal in federal court predictably restricts access to justice—especially for resource-constrained plaintiffs—by turning pre-suit expert access into a gate that the Federal Rules deliberately do not impose at filing, and that practical impact reinforces (rather than overrides) my reading that the Rules are sufficiently broad to control this procedural sequencing.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point remains the functional one: Delaware’s AOM operates as a front-loaded merits screen that looks like it intrudes on the Federal Rules’ pleading, dismissal, and amendment framework (Rules 8, 12, 15). But as Justice Barrett and Chief Justice Roberts emphasize, the Hanna/Burlington Northern threshold is whether a Federal Rule is sufficiently broad to answer the same question and leave no room for the state requirement, and Rule 11’s text expressly anticipating affidavits required by “a rule or statute” makes it hard to say the Rules categorically forbid state affidavit prerequisites. Walker’s logic, invoked by Justices Gorsuch and Alito, is persuasive here: absent a direct collision, a state-law condition tied to maintaining a state-created malpractice claim applies in diversity, and Erie’s twin aims strongly cut against creating an AOM-free federal bypass. Sotomayor’s access-to-justice concerns are real, but under a pragmatic textualist approach they don’t justify stretching the Federal Rules beyond their fair scope to displace a state gatekeeping condition the Rules can coherently accommodate.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right to emphasize that Delaware’s affidavit-of-merit functions as an early merits screen, but under Hanna and Burlington Northern the threshold question remains whether any Federal Rule is sufficiently broad to answer whether such a state-law precondition may be required, leaving no room for it to operate. As Justice Barrett persuasively notes, Rule 11’s text expressly contemplates affidavits when a “rule or statute” requires them, which strongly suggests the Federal Rules do not purport to preempt state verification prerequisites across the board. Walker, as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan argue, supplies the correct analytic posture: where the Federal Rules do not directly speak to the specific state condition for maintaining a state-created claim, Erie’s twin aims counsel applying the state rule to avoid an AOM-free federal bypass. Access-to-justice concerns are real, but they cannot justify rewriting the Rules’ scope; the proper remedy lies with Delaware’s policy choices or with state-law mechanisms for extension/waiver, not federal displacement absent a true collision.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right to press that Delaware’s AOM functions as a front-loaded merits screen and can look like a heightened pleading/dismissal device in tension with Rules 8, 12, and 15. But under Hanna and Burlington Northern, I agree with Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett that the threshold question is whether any Federal Rule is sufficiently broad to answer the same question and thereby displace Delaware’s condition on maintaining this state-created malpractice claim; fairly read, the Rules govern federal pleading and motion practice, not whether state law may require an expert-supported certification as a prerequisite to proceed. Barrett’s point about Rule 11 expressly contemplating affidavits required by “a rule or statute” is particularly powerful because it undercuts the idea that the Rules establish an exclusive, affidavit-free filing regime. With no direct collision, Walker and Erie’s twin aims strongly favor applying the AOM to avoid a predictable federal-court bypass and inequitable administration between state and federal forums.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point—that Delaware’s AOM functions as a front-loaded merits screen overlapping Rules 8, 12, and 15—does not establish a Hanna/Burlington Northern “direct collision” because none of those Rules answers the same question: whether state law may condition continuation of this state-created malpractice claim on timely expert support. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, we should construe the Federal Rules to avoid unnecessary displacement of state law, and Rule 11’s text (“unless a rule or statute specifically states otherwise”) affirmatively anticipates affidavit/verification requirements imposed outside the Rules, undermining the claim that the Rules create an exclusive federal filing regime that preempts the AOM. Walker, as Justice Gorsuch notes, reinforces that when the Rules do not speak to the precise issue, state law supplies the rule of decision in diversity, and Erie’s twin aims strongly favor applying the AOM to prevent an AOM-free federal bypass. Access-to-justice concerns are real, but under a textualist/originalist approach they cannot justify expanding the Rules’ scope beyond their terms to invalidate a state condition tied to the maintenance of a substantive state claim.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s collision argument is the hardest for me because Delaware’s AOM can operate as an access-limiting, front-loaded merits screen that resembles heightened federal gatekeeping. But under Hanna/Burlington Northern, I agree with Justice Barrett that Rule 11’s text—contemplating affidavits when “a rule or statute” requires them—materially weakens the claim that the Federal Rules establish an exclusive, no-affidavit regime that Delaware’s AOM necessarily displaces. Once the asserted “direct collision” is not persuasive, Walker’s logic (as emphasized by the Chief and Justice Kagan) makes the pragmatic Erie consequences decisive: refusing to apply the AOM would predictably create a federal-court bypass and invite forum shopping and inequitable administration. My procedural-fairness concern is better addressed through faithful application of Delaware’s own extension/waiver safety valves rather than by recharacterizing the Federal Rules to preempt the State’s gatekeeping condition.

John Roberts.reasoning: Under Hanna v. Plumer and Burlington Northern R.R. Co. v. Woods, the threshold question is whether any Federal Rule is “sufficiently broad” to control the issue and thus directly collide with Delaware’s AOM requirement. Properly construed, Rules 8, 9, 11, 12, 15, and 56 regulate pleading standards, sanctions, and motion practice, but do not purport to displace a state-law precondition to maintaining a medical-negligence claim—so we should interpret the Rules to avoid conflict with an important state regulatory policy (cf. Gasperini v. Center for Humanities, Inc.). With no direct collision, Erie R.R. Co. v. Tompkins and Hanna’s twin aims counsel enforcing the Delaware AOM statute to prevent forum shopping and inequitable administration of the laws (federal court as an AOM-free bypass), and a narrow holding preserves institutional legitimacy while respecting federalism. Shady Grove does not compel a different result here because it turned on Rule 23’s comprehensive governance of class certification, whereas no Federal Rule comprehensively governs state malpractice “certificate/affidavit of merit” screening prerequisites.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Federal Rules do not directly displace Delaware’s affidavit-of-merit requirement because no Rule is “sufficiently broad” to control the precise issue and leave “no room” for the state-law condition to operate. Burlington Northern R. Co. v. Woods supplies the controlling “direct collision” test, and Rule 11’s text expressly contemplates affidavit requirements imposed by “a rule or statute,” undermining any claim that Rules 8, 11, or 12 categorically forbid Delaware’s AOM prerequisite. Where there is no direct collision, Erie and Hanna require giving effect to state law that is bound up with the State’s allocation of rights and liabilities and that, if ignored, would predictably encourage forum shopping and produce inequitable administration of the laws. Applying Delaware’s AOM rule in diversity respects state authority over substantive medical-negligence policy choices and preserves the limited role of federal courts in diversity cases.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Delaware’s Affidavit of Merit requirement functions as a state-law condition on maintaining a medical-negligence claim, and the Federal Rules (Rules 8, 11, 12, 15, 56) do not “directly collide” with that gatekeeping device because they regulate pleading and motion practice, not state-created prerequisites to suit. Under the Erie/Hanna framework, where no Federal Rule squarely governs the same issue, the court should apply the state rule to avoid forum shopping and inequitable administration of the laws—otherwise plaintiffs could evade Delaware’s substantive screening policy by filing in federal court. This approach is consistent with Walker v. Armco Steel (state rule tied to the enforcement of the claim applies absent a direct collision) and Burlington Northern’s “direct collision” test, which Shady Grove did not displace. Enforcing the AOM also serves substantial state interests in deterring nonmeritorious malpractice claims and reducing unnecessary litigation costs, practical consequences that federal courts in diversity should respect.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Delaware’s AOM statute functions as an early merits-screening and dismissal trigger that, in federal court, collides with the Federal Rules’ integrated regime for commencing an action and testing its sufficiency—Rules 8 and 11 set the pleading and certification baseline, Rules 12 and 56 supply the mechanisms for early dismissal on legal or evidentiary insufficiency, and Rule 15 governs curing defects without forfeiting claims on technicalities. Under Hanna and Burlington Northern, when a Federal Rule is “sufficiently broad” to control the issue, the Rule governs; here, enforcing a state-law affidavit prerequisite as a condition to proceed would effectively impose a heightened filing requirement beyond the Rules’ calibrated system. Even under Shady Grove (including Justice Stevens’s approach), applying federal pleading/sanctions rules to permit the suit to proceed does not impermissibly abridge a substantive state right; it regulates the manner and timing of proving merit, not Delaware’s elements of medical negligence or defenses. Pragmatically, rigid AOM enforcement in diversity risks denying access to justice—especially for vulnerable plaintiffs facing time, cost, or access-to-expert barriers—by converting potentially meritorious claims into dismissals based on pre-discovery paperwork rather than adjudication on the merits.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Delaware’s AOM requirement functions as a state-law condition on maintaining a medical-negligence claim and does not “directly collide” with any Federal Rule because Rules 8, 9, 11, and 12 regulate pleading and sanctions, not a state-defined prerequisite to suit or early continuation. Under Burlington Northern and Walker, we ask whether the Federal Rules are “sufficiently broad” to control the issue and leave “no room” for state law; here they are not, so Erie’s twin aims matter. Refusing to apply the AOM would predictably invite forum shopping (federal court as an AOM-free bypass) and yield inequitable administration for Delaware malpractice defendants, so the federal court should enforce the Delaware requirement in diversity. Shady Grove does not alter this threshold collision inquiry; absent a collision, we apply the state rule that is bound up with the State’s allocation of rights and liabilities in this field.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Under Hanna v. Plumer and Burlington Northern Railroad Co. v. Woods, the threshold question is whether a Federal Rule "answers the question in dispute" and is sufficiently broad to create a direct collision with the Delaware AOM requirement. The Federal Rules (including Rules 8, 11, 12, and 56) govern pleading sufficiency, sanctions, motions to dismiss, and summary judgment, but they do not purport to eliminate state-law prerequisites that define when a medical-negligence claim may be maintained; thus there is room for the Delaware AOM statute to operate, much as in Walker v. Armco Steel Corp. where Rule 3 did not displace a state commencement rule tied to limitations. With no direct collision, Erie Railroad Co. v. Tompkins and its forum-shopping/inequitable-administration concerns counsel applying Delaware’s AOM requirement in diversity to avoid making federal court an AOM-free bypass for malpractice suits. Because the Federal Rules need not be extended to invalidate a state condition bound up with the State’s liability regime, this case can be resolved without invoking Shady Grove’s Rules Enabling Act inquiry.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Under Hanna and Burlington Northern, the first question is whether a Federal Rule “answers the same question” and is sufficiently broad to create a “direct collision” with Delaware’s Affidavit of Merit (AOM) requirement. Rules 8, 11, 12, 15, and 56 regulate pleading standards, sanctions, motions to dismiss, amendments, and summary judgment, but they do not purport to displace a state-law condition on maintaining a medical-negligence action—an early expert-support screen that Delaware has tied to the substantive enforcement of malpractice liability; this looks more like Walker, where the Federal Rules left room for the State’s litigation-triggering requirement. If no direct collision exists, Erie’s twin aims counsel applying the Delaware AOM rule because exempting diversity plaintiffs would invite forum shopping and produce inequitable administration by allowing an AOM-free federal bypass for malpractice suits. This approach also aligns with Shady Grove (Justice Stevens’ controlling concurrence) by avoiding an interpretation of the Federal Rules that would unnecessarily override a state rule closely bound up with substantive policy choices in a particular field.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Under Hanna v. Plumer and Shady Grove, the threshold question is whether a Federal Rule "answers the question in dispute" and thus directly collides with Delaware’s affidavit-of-merit requirement. No such collision exists because Rule 11’s text expressly contemplates affidavit requirements imposed by a "rule or statute" ("a pleading need not be verified or accompanied by an affidavit" unless one "specifically states otherwise"), leaving room for Delaware’s AOM as a condition to proceed in medical-negligence actions. Absent a directly applicable Federal Rule displacing the statute, Erie and its forum-shopping/inequitable-administration concerns counsel enforcing the Delaware AOM in diversity to avoid making federal court an AOM-free bypass of state malpractice policy. Walker v. Armco Steel reinforces that where the Federal Rules do not purport to govern the precise issue, state law supplies the rule of decision in diversity.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Under Hanna and Burlington Northern, the first question is whether a Federal Rule is “sufficiently broad” to control the issue and thus directly collide with Delaware’s AOM requirement; here, Rules 8, 9, 11, 12, 15, and 56 regulate pleading standards and litigation conduct but do not purport to eliminate state-law conditions on maintaining a medical-negligence claim, leaving room for the Delaware AOM statute to operate. In the absence of a direct collision, Erie and Walker counsel applying state law where ignoring it would be outcome-determinative and invite forum shopping and inequitable administration—precisely what would occur if plaintiffs could bypass Delaware’s AOM screen by filing in federal court. Delaware’s AOM operates as part of the State’s framework for enforcing and limiting medical-negligence liability (a practical gatekeeping condition), and enforcing it in diversity respects procedural fairness by treating similarly situated litigants the same regardless of forum. While the Federal Rules provide mechanisms to test plausibility and sanction frivolous claims, they do not clearly “answer the same question” as an expert-certification prerequisite tied to state substantive policy, so the state requirement should be enforced.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a federal court sitting in diversity must enforce Delaware’s affidavit-of-merit (AOM) requirement in a medical-negligence action, or whether the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure displace that state-law prerequisite.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Delaware’s medical-negligence affidavit-of-merit statute (the Delaware AOM requirement governing commencement/pleading of healthcare negligence claims) and its interaction with the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure (especially Rules 8, 9, 11, 12, and 3) under Erie/Hanna analysis.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Berk argues that Delaware’s AOM requirement is a state procedural screening device that conflicts with, and is therefore displaced by, the Federal Rules’ comprehensive pleading and sanctions framework (e.g., Rule 8 notice pleading and Rule 11 deterrence). He contends that forcing AOM compliance in federal court improperly adds a heightened, state-created gatekeeping condition to filing/maintaining a claim that the Federal Rules do not require, undermining uniform federal procedure and effectively imposing an extra-Rule dismissal mechanism. Under Hanna/Shady Grove, he maintains the Federal Rules control and the state AOM rule should not bar his federal-court malpractice claim.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Choy and Beebe Medical Center argue that Delaware’s AOM requirement is substantive (or at least outcome-determinative in the Erie sense) because it defines a prerequisite to a viable medical-negligence claim and reflects Delaware’s policy choice to deter non-meritorious suits, protect access to healthcare, and manage malpractice costs. They contend the AOM statute can be applied in federal court without contradicting the Federal Rules because it operates as a state-law element/condition of suit rather than a competing federal pleading standard. Under Erie and its twin aims (discouraging forum shopping and inequitable administration of the laws), they say federal courts must apply Delaware’s AOM requirement; otherwise plaintiffs would evade Delaware’s screening regime by choosing federal court.
key_precedents: Shady Grove Orthopedic Associates, P.A. v. Allstate Insurance Co.
Burlington Northern Railroad Co. v. Woods
Gasperini v. Center for Humanities, Inc.

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson press the best objection: that Delaware’s affidavit-of-merit adds a dismissal trigger beyond Rules 8, 11, and 12, creating the kind of “direct collision” Burlington Northern condemns. But I think that argument reads those Rules at too high a level of generality; as Justice Kagan and Justice Alito emphasize, read fairly under Hanna step one, the Rules govern pleading sufficiency, motions practice, and sanctions—not whether Delaware has defined a malpractice claim as not maintainable absent a contemporaneous expert attestation, which can operate side-by-side in the Walker sense. Burlington Northern involved a Federal Rule squarely addressing the same consequence and leaving no room for state supplementation, whereas here the Rules do not purport to supply an exclusive, comprehensive gatekeeping scheme for state-law conditions of suit. With no sufficiently on-point Rule, Erie’s twin aims favor applying Delaware’s requirement to avoid forum shopping and inequitable administration, consistent with Shady Grove’s (Stevens) caution against displacing closely claim-linked state provisions absent a true collision.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson argue that Rules 8, 11, and 12 form an integrated federal screening scheme, so Delaware’s affidavit-of-merit necessarily “collides” by adding a new dismissal trigger. But that frames the Rules at too high a level of generality: read textually and fairly, those Rules address what a complaint must contain, how a defendant may test it, and when sanctions are appropriate—not whether state law may define a malpractice claim as not maintainable absent a contemporaneous expert attestation. Chief Justice Roberts’s reliance on Walker is persuasive on this point: like Rule 3 in Walker, the Federal Rules can operate “side by side” with a state condition tied to the availability of the state-created right, and Burlington Northern is distinguishable because it involved a Federal Rule squarely governing the same penalty question and leaving no room for the state add-on. With no direct collision, Erie’s twin aims and the absence of any Rules Enabling Act warrant for construing the Rules to negate state-law prerequisites confirm that Delaware’s requirement applies in diversity.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s and Justice Jackson’s best point is that Delaware’s affidavit-of-merit operates as an early, dismissal-triggering filing prerequisite and thus practically adds to the Rules 8/11/12 screening scheme, invoking Burlington Northern’s “direct collision” language. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas stress, Hanna’s first step asks whether a Federal Rule, read fairly rather than at a high level of abstraction, answers the same question—none of Rules 8, 11, or 12 purports to foreclose state-law conditions precedent tied to the maintainability of a state-created malpractice claim, so the regimes can operate “side by side” in Walker’s sense. Burlington Northern is distinguishable because the Federal Rule there directly regulated the same sanction/penalty subject and left no room for the state overlay, whereas here Rule 11’s sanction standard and Rule 12’s dismissal grounds do not create an affirmative entitlement to proceed absent compliance with Delaware’s prerequisite. With no unavoidable collision, Erie’s twin aims carry substantial weight: ignoring the AOM would predictably invite forum shopping and inequitable administration of Delaware’s medical-malpractice regime.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s Walker framing is the strongest counter: if the Federal Rules don’t “answer the question” of Delaware’s condition-of-suit, the regimes can run side by side and Erie’s twin aims would favor the affidavit. But unlike Walker’s classic tolling/limitations consequence, Delaware’s AOM functions as an automatic, front-end dismissal trigger keyed to what must accompany the complaint, effectively supplanting the Federal Rules’ calibrated choices (Rules 8 and 12 for pleading and early dismissal, and Rule 11 for post-filing deterrence) by creating an additional federal-court filing hurdle. Burlington Northern is relevant because it treats state-law procedural add-ons that prescribe dismissal-type consequences at a stage the Federal Rules already govern as displaced when a Rule occupies that field; here, applying Delaware’s AOM in federal court imposes a separate pleading-screen not contemplated by the Rules’ integrated scheme. Justice Kagan’s “read the Rules fairly, not broadly” point understates the real-world collision and access-to-justice costs: plaintiffs who comply with federal pleading and certification obligations can still be turned away solely for missing a state-mandated affidavit, a procedural gate that disproportionately burdens those with fewer resources without changing the substantive standard of care.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson press a serious “integrated federal screening regime” theory—i.e., that Rules 8, 11, and 12 collectively answer what is required to file and survive the outset, so Delaware’s affidavit-of-merit adds a dismissal trigger and thus collides under Hanna/Burlington Northern. But that framing reads those Rules at too high a level of generality: fairly read, they set federal pleading standards, motion practice, and sanction consequences; they do not purport to confer an entitlement to maintain a state-created malpractice action without satisfying a state-law condition precedent tied to the claim’s permissible maintenance (Walker’s side-by-side logic fits better than Burlington Northern’s true on-point Rule). Under Shady Grove (Stevens), we should hesitate to construe the Rules to displace a state’s calibrated access-to-remedy limit absent a clear textual conflict, and applying the AOM in diversity better serves Erie’s twin aims by avoiding predictable forum shopping around Delaware’s screening policy. I therefore remain with the Respondent.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson press the best objection: that Rules 8, 11, and 12 form an integrated federal screening scheme and Delaware’s affidavit-of-merit creates an additional, complaint-stage dismissal trigger, akin to a “direct collision” under Hanna and Burlington Northern. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas emphasize, Hanna’s first step asks whether a Federal Rule, read fairly and at the right level of specificity, answers the same question; Rules 8/12 govern what must be pleaded and how pleadings are tested, and Rule 11 governs sanctions for improper filings, none of which purports to negate a State’s substantive condition on maintaining a state-created medical-negligence claim. Walker remains the closer fit because it recognizes state prerequisites that can operate “side by side” with the Federal Rules when the Rules do not speak to the claim’s state-law viability conditions. Shady Grove (particularly Justice Stevens’s approach) reinforces that we should not construe the Rules to displace such a state calibration absent an unavoidable conflict, and Erie’s twin aims counsel applying Delaware’s requirement to avoid forum shopping and inequitable administration.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson press the best objection: Delaware’s affidavit-of-merit operates as an extra, mandatory early-dismissal trigger that looks like a state-added pleading screen atop Rules 8, 11, and 12. But under the “read fairly, not broadly” approach Chief Justice Roberts outlines (and consistent with Walker), those Federal Rules regulate the content and testing of pleadings and sanctioning of improper filings; they do not purport to answer the distinct question whether Delaware may make a contemporaneous expert attestation a condition of maintaining this state-created malpractice claim, so the regimes can operate side by side. Burlington Northern is distinguishable because the Federal Rule there squarely governed the same subject and left no room for the state penalty, whereas here no Rule is sufficiently on point to displace the state prerequisite. With no direct collision, Erie’s twin aims favor applying the Delaware requirement to avoid predictable forum shopping and inequitable administration of Delaware’s substantive screening policy.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor (and Justice Jackson) persuasively frame the affidavit-of-merit as an added, dismissal-triggering pleading screen that could be said to "collide" with Rules 8, 11, and 12. But under Hanna’s first step the relevant question must be stated at the right level of generality, and—consistent with Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s Walker analogy—the Federal Rules, read fairly, regulate the sufficiency of allegations and sanctions for improper filings; they do not purport to answer whether state law may define a state-created malpractice claim as not maintainable absent a contemporaneous expert attestation. Burlington Northern involved a Federal Rule that squarely occupied the same subject and left no room for the state consequence, whereas here the AOM can operate side-by-side as a state-law precondition without altering what Rule 8 requires to plead. With no direct collision, Erie’s twin aims point strongly toward applying the AOM to avoid forum shopping and inequitable administration.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s Walker v. Armco Steel analogy is the strongest counter: that the Federal Rules can be read “fairly” to leave room for a state condition of suit, triggering Erie’s twin aims. But I don’t think Delaware’s affidavit-of-merit functions like Walker’s tolling/commencement rule; it is a pleadings-stage, mandatory, dismissal-triggering filing prerequisite that effectively retools the threshold federal screening regime established by Rules 8, 11, and 12, creating the kind of practical collision Burlington Northern and Hanna treat as displacement-worthy. Justice Kagan’s “side-by-side” framing assumes the Rules are silent on whether a plaintiff who satisfies Rule 8 may nevertheless be dismissed for failing to attach extra state-required materials, but in my view the Rules do answer that question by specifying what must be filed and when dismissal is available at the outset, leaving sanctions and later merits proof (including expert evidence) to other stages. Under Shady Grove (including Justice Stevens’s focus on whether the Rule truly regulates procedure), applying the FRCP here governs the manner and means of litigating in federal court without redefining Delaware’s substantive standard of care, while importing the affidavit gatekeeping risks turning a state procedural screen into a federal courthouse-door barrier.

John Roberts.reasoning: Under Hanna v. Plumer and Burlington Northern R.R. Co. v. Woods, the threshold question is whether any Federal Rule is “sufficiently broad” to create a direct collision with Delaware’s affidavit-of-merit prerequisite. Rules 8, 9, 11, 12, and 3 regulate federal pleading, sanctions, motions to dismiss, and commencement, but they do not squarely answer the distinct state-law question whether a medical-negligence claim is viable absent a contemporaneous expert attestation; there is thus room for the Delaware AOM requirement to operate without displacing the Federal Rules (cf. Walker v. Armco Steel Corp.). Applying the AOM requirement also serves Erie’s twin aims by preventing forum shopping and inequitable administration, since ignoring it would allow plaintiffs to evade Delaware’s substantive screening policy simply by choosing federal court. This is a narrow, precedent-aligned resolution that preserves institutional legitimacy by avoiding an unnecessary holding that the Rules Enabling Act invalidates or overrides Delaware’s chosen condition on suit (Shady Grove (Stevens, J., controlling)).

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Properly read, the Federal Rules do not "answer the question in dispute"—whether Delaware conditions the viability of a medical-negligence action on filing an affidavit of merit—so there is no "direct collision" under Hanna and Shady Grove. As in Walker v. Armco Steel, Rule 3 (and likewise Rules 8, 9, 11, and 12) can be "read fairly" to leave room for a State’s substantive condition of suit, allowing the federal and state requirements to "exist side by side" without conflict. Applying Delaware’s AOM requirement in diversity also serves Erie’s twin aims by preventing forum shopping and avoiding inequitable administration of the laws, since ignoring the AOM would invite plaintiffs to evade Delaware’s screening regime by choosing federal court. Because the AOM statute reflects Delaware’s policy judgment about the prerequisites to maintaining a malpractice claim, a federal court sitting in diversity should enforce it absent a truly unavoidable conflict with a Federal Rule.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Delaware’s affidavit-of-merit statute operates as a state-law condition on maintaining a medical-negligence action and reflects a substantive policy choice to deter meritless malpractice claims; ignoring it in diversity would invite forum shopping and inequitable administration of the laws under Erie. Under Hanna’s first step, the Federal Rules must be read fairly, not broadly, and displace state law only when they are “sufficiently broad” to create a “direct collision” leaving “no room” for the state provision; here, Rules 8, 9, 11, 12, and 3 do not specifically answer whether a malpractice plaintiff must supply an expert affidavit as a precondition to suit. Walker v. Armco Steel confirms that when a Federal Rule (there, Rule 3) does not purport to govern the same question as the state condition (tolling/commencement), the state requirement applies, and similar reasoning allows the AOM rule and Rule 11 to “exist side by side” without conflict. Applying Delaware’s AOM requirement in federal court therefore best respects state substantive policy and the practical consequences for healthcare providers while remaining consistent with the Rules Enabling Act limits recognized in Shady Grove and Burlington Northern.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Delaware’s affidavit-of-merit requirement functions as a gatekeeping prerequisite to filing/maintaining a malpractice claim and directly collides with the Federal Rules’ integrated pleading and sanctions regime—particularly Rules 8 and 12 (governing what must be pleaded and when dismissal is proper) and Rule 11 (deterring nonmeritorious filings). Under Hanna and Burlington Northern, when a Federal Rule is sufficiently broad to control the issue and valid under the Rules Enabling Act, it governs in diversity; applying Delaware’s AOM would add a heightened, state-created dismissal trigger not found in the Rules. Consistent with Justice Stevens’s controlling approach in Shady Grove, the Federal Rules here operate as general rules of practice and procedure and enforcing them does not impermissibly abridge substantive rights, while the AOM requirement risks denying access to court—especially for vulnerable plaintiffs—based on an extra federal-court filing hurdle. Therefore, the Federal Rules displace the Delaware AOM prerequisite in federal court.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Under Hanna and Shady Grove, the first question is whether any Federal Rule is “sufficiently broad” to answer the same question as Delaware’s AOM statute and thus leave “no room” for it; read fairly rather than broadly, Rules 8, 9, 11, 12, and 3 regulate federal pleading, sanctions, and commencement, but they do not purport to displace a state-law condition precedent to maintaining a medical-negligence claim. Walker v. Armco Steel instructs that Rule 3 did not override a state tolling rule because the Rule did not control the specific issue; similarly, Delaware’s AOM requirement (a prerequisite designed to screen malpractice claims, 18 Del. C. § 6853) can operate alongside the Federal Rules without a direct collision. With no on-point Federal Rule, Erie’s twin aims favor applying the AOM requirement because exempting federal diversity plaintiffs would invite forum shopping and create inequitable administration of Delaware’s malpractice regime. That outcome also best respects Delaware’s policy choice to define the practical availability of its medical-negligence cause of action while keeping federal procedure intact.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Under Hanna and Shady Grove, the first question is whether a Federal Rule “answers the question in dispute” and is sufficiently broad to create a “direct collision” with the Delaware affidavit-of-merit prerequisite. Rules 8, 9, 11, 12, and 3 regulate pleading, sanctions, motions, and when an action is commenced, but none purports to eliminate a State’s substantive precondition to maintaining a medical-negligence claim; as in Walker v. Armco Steel, Rule 3 does not displace a state-law condition tied to the viability of the cause of action. Because there is no direct collision, Erie’s twin aims counsel applying Delaware’s AOM requirement to avoid incentivizing forum shopping and inequitable administration of the laws (Gasperini). Enforcing the AOM statute thus respects state substantive policy choices without rewriting the Federal Rules or expanding judicially created federal procedural power at the expense of state law.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Under Hanna and Shady Grove, the threshold question is whether any Federal Rule is “sufficiently broad” to control the issue and thereby create a direct collision with Delaware’s affidavit-of-merit prerequisite. As in Walker v. Armco Steel Corp., Rules 3, 8, 9, 11, and 12 do not purport to answer whether state law may require a pre-suit or filing-adjacent certification as a condition of maintaining a medical-negligence claim, so the state and federal regimes can “exist side by side” without conflict. With no direct collision, Erie’s twin aims point toward applying the Delaware AOM requirement because ignoring it in diversity would invite forum shopping and produce inequitable administration by allowing plaintiffs to evade Delaware’s screening condition in federal court. This approach also promotes practical workability and respect for state policy choices in defining the prerequisites to liability in a sensitive area of traditional state regulation.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Applying the Burlington/Walker framework, the Federal Rules do not “answer the question in dispute” because none of Rules 3, 8, 9, 11, or 12 purports to authorize commencement of a Delaware medical-negligence action without satisfying a state-law condition of suit; Delaware’s affidavit-of-merit requirement instead operates as a prerequisite to a viable malpractice claim. Where the Federal Rules are not “sufficiently broad to cause a direct collision” with the state law, Erie requires applying the state rule to avoid forum shopping and inequitable administration of the laws. See Burlington N. R.R. Co. v. Woods, 480 U.S. 1, 4–5 (1987); Walker v. Armco Steel Corp., 446 U.S. 740, 750–53 (1980). Because disregarding the AOM would allow plaintiffs to evade Delaware’s screening regime by choosing federal court, Erie’s twin aims favor enforcement in diversity, and Shady Grove does not alter that conclusion absent a genuine FRCP collision.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Under Hanna v. Plumer and Shady Grove, the first question is whether the Federal Rules “answer the question in dispute”—here, what a plaintiff must file to commence and maintain a malpractice action and avoid dismissal at the pleading stage. Federal Rules 3 and 8 set a uniform commencement and notice-pleading regime, while Rules 11 and 12 provide the federal mechanisms for screening and sanctioning insufficient or nonmeritorious claims; Delaware’s affidavit-of-merit prerequisite operates as an extra, state-created gatekeeping condition that triggers dismissal notwithstanding compliance with those Rules, creating the kind of direct collision described in Burlington Northern. Because the Federal Rules are valid rules of practice and procedure under the Rules Enabling Act as applied here (they regulate the manner and means of enforcing rights rather than defining the underlying standard of care), they displace Delaware’s AOM requirement in federal diversity cases. This approach also promotes procedural fairness by preventing a heightened, front-end barrier to court access that the Federal Rules do not impose, particularly where dismissal can function as a merits-ending penalty unrelated to the adequacy of the federal pleading.
